title: Check whether docs work for AI agents
promise: Scan a documentation URL for common access and format problems, then review a scorecard.
whatItIs: Velu's agent-friendly documentation checker is described as scoring a documentation URL against the open Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec, using the spec's reference implementation called afdocs. The Show HN post names issues the spec is concerned with: pages rendered only in the browser, missing llms.txt or Markdown versions, soft 404 pages, and pages too large for an agent's context window. A beginner could build a small scheduled checker for one documentation site that records the score and lists detectable problems. Documentation teams are a plausible customer, but the source does not establish who pays. This is an audit and reporting loop, not an automatic documentation repair service.
whoPays: Hypothesis: teams maintaining developer documentation may pay for recurring checks; the source does not establish customers or revenue.
loop: Read a configured documentation site URL.
Check pages for supported agent access and format signals.
Run the reference checker and save its score.
Compare the result with the previous scan.
Send a report when the score or detected issues change.
A documentation owner verifies findings and chooses any fix.
evidence: The Show HN description says Velu's tool scores documentation URLs against the open Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec using its reference implementation, afdocs. The author identifies client-rendered pages, missing llms.txt or Markdown, soft 404s, and oversized pages as problems the spec addresses.
uncertainty: This is a maker's description; the snapshot does not include an independent test or performance data. A student checker can only detect a limited set of public signals and may misclassify sites. A human should verify a finding before editing a documentation site.
first24Hours: Select a public documentation site and inspect the referenced open specification and checker interface.
Implement checks for one or two signals such as Markdown availability and obvious 404 responses.
Save a timestamped report and compare it with a second scan for changes.
